items_missed: No agenda statement — opened straight into 'how can I help you?' and never laid out the roadmap, the 10-15 minute timeframe, or asked 'sound good?'
Never asked 'how are you today?' — went from name capture directly to the ask

Probing was thin: got zips, 800 sqft/1BR, and first-floor-to-first-floor, then stopped. No garage/storage/balcony, no packing needs, no box count, no additional stops, no parking or access questions, no long-walk or narrow-hallway check

Never asked the moving-stressor question, even though the customer opened the call with a real stressor (pest treatment in her apartment) — the perfect opening for 'is there anything you're particularly worried about?'
Quoted a firm $520-$728 without ever asking how many boxes there are — the estimate is unsupported guesswork
No Worries Damage Coverage never explained — said 'insurance' is included and left it there, no $2,000 figure, no 60 cents/lb baseline
Packing service never offered or priced
Never said the clock starts on-site when the contract opens
No sense-check after the clock explanation — the customer had to interrupt to ask 'wait, three hour minimum?' and correct herself
Trucks not mentioned in the estimate (only 'two movers')
Entire Save Your Ass prep speech absent — no prep-equals-shorter-move framing, no consolidation examples, no take-a-carload tip
No booking attempt. Said 'we have availability right now' and never asked to lock it in; the customer left with 'I will call back and get things situated' — a live, ready-to-book lead walked
No deposit never mentioned — a differentiator that costs nothing to say
No confirmation email promised, no bolded-details list, no 'reply with any corrections'
Never asked 'any other questions before I let you go?' and never gave hours or how to reach us
Customer's name used only twice ('Hi Sarah', 'so Sarah for the safety')
top_strength: She handled the pest-treatment disclosure cleanly and without hedging — stated the policy plainly ('for the safety of our movers we don't let them go into any property that has an ongoing bug infestation'), then immediately gave the customer the path forward ('we can definitely help you out, but you need to give us just a written document from the exterminators that the apartment is clean or clear'). That is exactly the right handling of an awkward disclosure: no judgment, no dead end. She also surfaced the Sunday-through-Thursday discount days when asked and reassured the customer twice that she only pays for actual time used, which is honest, budget-conscious framing.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: ask for the booking. This customer was ready — she had picked dates (Sept 7 or 8), accepted the price, and thanked Danah for her time; Danah's own words were 'we have availability right now' and then nothing. The close should have been: 'Great news, we do have the 7th and the 8th open. There's no deposit to book, so let's go ahead and lock in the 8th for you and I'll send a confirmation email you can reply to with any corrections.' Second priority: stop quoting before you've probed. She gave a firm dollar range having never asked about boxes, packing, parking, or walk distance — that is how estimate accuracy stays at 52%. Add the four questions that actually move the clock (box count, packing needs, walk from door to truck, anything oversized) before any number leaves her mouth. Third, the differentiators are free and she skipped all three — No Worries $2,000 coverage, Meet Your Mover, and the On-Time Guarantee should be a fixed block right after 'no hidden fees,' not optional.
phone_presence_notes: Polite and non-judgmental on a sensitive disclosure, and the customer ended warm ('thank you so much, I really appreciate your time'), but the language was transactional throughout — heavy 'Mm-hmm'/'Yup' backchannel, no empathy statement acknowledging how stressful the pest situation clearly was, and no rapport beyond the task.
audio_review_reason: Heavy ASR garbling across the rep's core pricing delivery ('notice assembly and reassembly fee', 'general code for a one bedroom') and the customer interrupting to re-ask the minimum suggest possible pace or clarity problems that the transcript alone cannot confirm.
